text:
An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements.

[latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: A hash index must be a dense index
[latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: A [latex]B^{+}[/latex] tree index can be a sparse index

Which one of the following options is correct?
solution:
S1 (hash index must be dense): A hash index computes a bucket location directly from the key via a hash function; there is no notion of "sorted order" to allow skipping entries the way a sparse index can, so a hash index inherently needs a separate index entry pointing to the data for every distinct search-key value. True.

S2 ([latex]B^+[/latex]-tree can be sparse): When the [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index is built on a search key that also determines the physical sorted order of the underlying data file (i.e. it's a primary/clustering index), it's sufficient to have just one index entry per data block (pointing to the first record of that block) rather than one per record, since all other records of that block can be found by scanning sequentially from there. This makes a sparse [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index entirely feasible. True.

Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true.

text:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set [latex]\text{F}[/latex] of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by [latex]\text{F}[/latex] is called the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex]. To compute the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex], Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider [latex]X, Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If [latex]Y \subseteq X[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex]
Augmentation: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex], then [latex]X Z \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] for any Z
Transitivity: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]Y \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex]

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y Z[/latex]

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?
solution:
The standard proof of the Union rule ([latex]X\to Y,\,X\to Z\;\Rightarrow\;X\to YZ[/latex]) proceeds as follows:

1. [latex]X\to Y[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]X[/latex] to both sides): [latex]X\to XY[/latex] (using [latex]XX=X[/latex]).
2. [latex]X\to Z[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]Y[/latex] to both sides): [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex].
3. Combining steps 1 and 2 via Transitivity: [latex]X\to XY[/latex] and [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex] gives [latex]X\to YZ[/latex].

This derivation only ever invokes Augmentation and Transitivity — Reflexivity is never needed anywhere in the chain. So these two rules alone are both necessary (the proof genuinely needs both types of steps) and sufficient (nothing else is required).

Answer: Augmentation and Transitivity

text: Consider concurrent execution of two transactions [latex]T 1[/latex] and [latex]T 2[/latex] in a DBMS, both of which access a data object [latex]A[/latex]. For these two transactions to not conflict on [latex]A[/latex], which one of the following statements must be true?
solution:
Two operations by different transactions on the same data object [latex]A[/latex] "conflict" (in the standard DBMS concurrency-control sense) precisely when at least one of them is a write — i.e. any of read-write, write-read, or write-write pairs are conflicting, because the order in which they execute can change the outcome.

The only combination that never conflicts is when both transactions merely read [latex]A[/latex] — reads never interfere with each other regardless of execution order, since neither changes the value of [latex]A[/latex].

Answer: Both T1 and T2 only read A.

In the context of DBMS, consider the two sets [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] and [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] given below.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\quad\textbf{T} & \quad\quad\quad\textbf{S} \\ \hline \text{I: Logical schema} & \text{L: Views} \\ \text{II: Physical schema} & \text{M: File organization and indexes} \\ \text{III: External schema} & \text{N: Relations} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct match from [latex]\mathbf{T}[/latex] to [latex]\mathbf{S}[/latex] ?
solution:
Matching each schema level in the three-tier DBMS architecture to what it describes:

- Logical schema (I): describes the overall logical structure of the database for the whole community of users — this is exactly what relations (N) capture.
- Physical schema (II): describes how data is actually stored at the lowest level — file organization and indexes (M).
- External schema (III): describes a customized, user-specific way of seeing part of the data — exactly what views (L) provide.

Answer: I-N, II-M, III-L

text: Consider a relational database schema with a relation [latex]R(A, B, C, D)[/latex]. If [latex]\{A, B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A, C\}[/latex] are the only two candidate keys of the relation [latex]R[/latex], then the number of superkeys of relation [latex]R[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
solution:
A superkey is any subset of attributes that contains at least one candidate key as a subset. Here the [latex]4[/latex] attributes are [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex] and the candidate keys are [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex].

Count subsets of [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex] containing [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{C,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets.
Count subsets containing [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex]: freely choose the remaining [latex]\{B,D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^2=4[/latex] subsets.
Subsets counted twice are those containing both [latex]\{A,B\}[/latex] and [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex], i.e. containing [latex]\{A,B,C\}[/latex]: freely choose remaining [latex]\{D\}[/latex] → [latex]2^1=2[/latex] subsets.

By inclusion-exclusion, total superkeys [latex]=4+4-2=6[/latex].

Answer: 6

text:
Consider a relational database schema with two relations [latex]R(P, Q)[/latex] and [latex]S(X, Y)[/latex]. Let [latex]E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v \exists w\langle u, v\rangle \in R \wedge\langle v, w\rangle \in S\}[/latex] be a tuple relational calculus expression.
Which one of the following relational algebraic expressions is equivalent to [latex]E[/latex] ?
solution:
The calculus expression [latex]E=\{\langle u\rangle \mid \exists v\,\exists w\,\langle u,v\rangle\in R \wedge \langle v,w\rangle\in S\}[/latex] asks for all [latex]u[/latex] such that some tuple [latex]\langle u,v\rangle[/latex] is in [latex]R[/latex] and that same [latex]v[/latex] appears as the first component of some tuple [latex]\langle v,w\rangle[/latex] in [latex]S[/latex].

This is a natural join of [latex]R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] where [latex]R[/latex]'s second attribute ([latex]Q[/latex], which plays the role of [latex]v[/latex]) matches [latex]S[/latex]'s first attribute ([latex]X[/latex], which also plays the role of [latex]v[/latex]): join condition [latex]R.Q=S.X[/latex]. After joining, we only want the value of [latex]u[/latex], i.e. project onto [latex]P[/latex].

So [latex]E\equiv\Pi_P\big(S\bowtie_{S.X=R.Q}R\big)[/latex] (the join is symmetric, so writing [latex]S[/latex] first or [latex]R[/latex] first with the same condition gives the same relation).

Answer: [latex]\Pi_P\left(S\bowtie_{S.X=R.Q}R\right)[/latex]

text: In the context of relational database normalization, which of the following statements is/are true?
solution:
Standard relational-normalization theory results:

- 3NF: It is a classical theorem that every relation schema has a dependency-preserving (and lossless-join) decomposition into 3NF, via the synthesis algorithm on a minimal cover of the FDs. True.
- 1NF: 1NF only requires atomic domains; a relation can always trivially satisfy/preserve 1NF without needing to give up any functional dependency (no decomposition is even forced). True.
- BCNF: It is a well-known counterexample-backed result that a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition is not always possible — achieving BCNF can force us to lose some functional dependency (they can only be checked by joining relations back together, which is expensive/impossible to enforce locally). True (i.e., "not always possible" is a true statement).
- 2NF: Since a dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition always exists, and 3NF automatically implies 2NF, a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition is always achievable too. So "it is not always possible to get a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition" is false.

Answer: Dependency-preserving decompositions always exist for 3NF and for 1NF; it is not always possible for BCNF.

text:
Let [latex]P, Q, R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] be the attributes of a relation in a relational schema. Let [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] indicate functional dependency in the context of a relational database, where [latex]X, Y \subseteq\{P, Q, R, S\}[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are always true?
solution:
Using Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) to test each claim:

- {P,Q}→{R} and {P}→{R}, does {Q}→{R} follow? No — {P}→{R} already implies {P,Q}→{R} by augmentation, so the premises give no information forcing {Q}→{R} to hold. Not always true.
- {P,Q}→{R}, does {P}→{R} or {Q}→{R} follow? No — {R} may genuinely require both P and Q together (e.g. R functionally depends on the pair but on neither attribute alone). Not always true.
- {P}→{R} and {Q}→{S}, does {P,Q}→{R,S} follow? Yes: augment {P}→{R} with Q to get {P,Q}→{R,Q}; augment {Q}→{S} with P to get {P,Q}→{P,S}; using reflexivity ({R,Q}→{R} and {P,S}→{S}) and transitivity gives {P,Q}→{R} and {P,Q}→{S}; the union rule then gives {P,Q}→{R,S}. Always true.
- {P}→{R}, does {P,Q}→{R} follow? Yes, directly by the augmentation axiom (adding Q to the left-hand side of a valid FD keeps it valid). Always true.

Answer: {P}→{R},{Q}→{S} &there4 {P,Q}→{R,S}; and {P}→{R} &there4 {P,Q}→{R}.

text:
Consider the following relational schema:

[latex] \text{Students} (\text{\underline{rollno: integer,} name: string, age: integer, cgpa: real}) [/latex]
[latex] \text{Courses} (\text{\underline{courseno: integer,} cname: string, credits: integer}) [/latex]
[latex] \text{Enrolled} (\text{ \underline{rollno: integer,} \underline{courseno: integer,} grade: string}) [/latex]

Which of the following options is/are correct SQL query/queries to retrieve the names of the students enrolled in course number (i.e. courseno) 1470?
solution:
All of the standard relational-algebra-equivalent SQL formulations for "students who have an Enrolled row with courseno=1470" are valid: using [latex]\text{EXISTS}[/latex] with a correlated subquery, using [latex]\text{COUNT(*)} > 0[/latex] in place of EXISTS (logically identical test), and using a [latex]\text{NATURAL JOIN}[/latex] between Students and Enrolled (which automatically joins on the shared [latex]rollno[/latex] column) filtered by courseno — all three correctly retrieve the same set of names.

The option using [latex]\text{SIZEOF}[/latex] is not valid: standard SQL has no [latex]\text{SIZEOF}[/latex] operator/function for comparing subquery result sizes this way (that's not real SQL syntax).

Answer: The EXISTS query, the COUNT(*)>0 query, and the NATURAL JOIN query are all correct.

options: SELECT S.name FROM Students S WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470 AND E.rollno = S.rollno)
SELECT S.name FROM Students S WHERE SIZEOF (SELECT * FROM Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470 AND E.rollno = S.rollno) > 0
SELECT S.name FROM Students S WHERE 0 < (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470 AND E.rollno = S.rollno)
SELECT S.name FROM Students S NATURAL JOIN Enrolled E WHERE E.courseno = 1470

text:
Consider the database transactions [latex]T1 [/latex] and [latex]T2 [/latex], and data items [latex]X [/latex] and [latex]Y [/latex]. Which of the schedule(s) is/are conflict serializable?

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T1} \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(Y) \\ \hline R1(X) \\ \hline W1(X) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T1)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|} \hline \textbf{Transaction T2} \\ \hline W2(X) \\ \hline W2(Y) \\ \hline \text{COMMIT(T2)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
solution:
Build the conflict/precedence graph for each schedule (an edge [latex]T_i\to T_j[/latex] whenever an operation of [latex]T_i[/latex] on some data item precedes a conflicting operation of [latex]T_j[/latex] on the same item, with at least one being a write); the schedule is conflict serializable iff this graph has no cycle.

Checking [latex]R1(X),W2(X),W1(Y),W2(Y),R1(X),W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: the first [latex]R1(X)[/latex] before [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T1\to T2[/latex], but the later [latex]R1(X)[/latex] appearing after [latex]W2(X)[/latex] gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] — a cycle. Not serializable.

Checking [latex]W2(X),R1(X),W2(Y),W1(Y),R1(X),\ldots,W1(X),\ldots[/latex]: every conflicting pair consistently gives [latex]T2\to T1[/latex] (write-then-read on [latex]X[/latex] first, write-then-write on [latex]Y[/latex], and the final [latex]W1(X)[/latex] happens safely after [latex]T2[/latex] has already committed) — no cycle. Conflict serializable.

The other two schedules can be checked the same way and each produces a cycle (conflicting edges pointing in both directions between T1 and T2).

Answer: Only "W2(X), R1(X), W2(Y), W1(Y), R1(X), COMMIT(T2), W1(X), COMMIT(T1)" is conflict serializable.

text:
Consider the following relational schema along with all the functional dependencies that hold on them.

[latex] R1(A, B, C, D, E): \{ D \to E, EA \to B, EB \to C \} [/latex]
[latex] R2(A, B, C, D): \{ A \to D, A \to B, C \to A \} [/latex]

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
solution:
[latex]R1(A,B,C,D,E)[/latex]: [latex]\{D\to E,\ EA\to B,\ EB\to C\}[/latex]. Computing candidate keys: [latex]\{A,D\}^+[/latex]: [latex]D\to E[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,D,E\}[/latex]; then [latex]EA\to B[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,B,D,E\}[/latex]; then [latex]EB\to C[/latex] gives all of [latex]\{A,B,C,D,E\}[/latex]. So [latex]\{A,D\}[/latex] is the (only, minimal) candidate key.
Check [latex]D\to E[/latex] against 3NF: is [latex]D[/latex] a superkey? No ([latex]D[/latex] alone only reaches [latex]\{D,E\}[/latex]). Is [latex]E[/latex] a prime attribute (part of some candidate key)? No (the only key is [latex]\{A,D\}[/latex], which doesn't include [latex]E[/latex]). Since neither condition holds, this FD violates 3NF. R1 is NOT in 3NF.

[latex]R2(A,B,C,D)[/latex]: [latex]\{A\to D,\ A\to B,\ C\to A\}[/latex]. [latex]\{C\}^+[/latex]: [latex]C\to A[/latex] gives [latex]\{A,C\}[/latex]; then [latex]A\to D,A\to B[/latex] gives all of [latex]\{A,B,C,D\}[/latex]. So [latex]\{C\}[/latex] alone is the candidate key.
Check [latex]A\to D[/latex]: is [latex]A[/latex] a superkey? No ([latex]A[/latex] alone reaches [latex]\{A,B,D\}[/latex], missing [latex]C[/latex]). Is [latex]D[/latex] prime? No (key is just [latex]\{C\}[/latex]). This FD also violates 3NF. R2 is NOT in 3NF.

Answer: R1 is NOT in 3NF; and R2 is NOT in 3NF.

text:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account [latex]A [/latex] attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account [latex]A [/latex] to account [latex]B [/latex]. Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in [latex]A [/latex] and were allowed to go through. [latex]B [/latex] was credited Rs. 10000 twice. [latex]A [/latex] was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.
Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?
solution:
This is a classic lost-update anomaly caused by two transactions reading the same stale value and overwriting each other's effects.

- Consistency is violated: the database ends up in a state that breaks the intended invariant (money should be conserved / correctly transferred), since [latex]A[/latex] should have ended up [latex]11000-20000[/latex] worth adjusted correctly but instead only one debit actually applied while both credits landed — the books don't balance as intended.
- Isolation is violated: the two concurrent transactions were not properly isolated from each other — both read [latex]A[/latex]'s balance before either had committed its update, letting their effects clash (textbook lost-update problem).
- Atomicity is not necessarily violated: each individual transaction ran to completion in full (no partial execution of a single transaction occurred).
- Durability is unrelated here: there's no indication of any committed-then-lost data due to a crash.

Answer: Consistency and Isolation

Consider a relational schema [latex] team(name, city, owner) [/latex], with functional dependencies [latex]\{ name \to city [/latex], [latex] name \to owner \} [/latex] .

The relation [latex] team [/latex] is decomposed into two relations, [latex] t_1(name, city) [/latex] and [latex] t_2(name, owner) [/latex]. Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
solution:
[latex]team(name,city,owner)[/latex] with [latex]name\to city,\ name\to owner[/latex]. Since [latex]name[/latex] alone functionally determines every other attribute, [latex]name[/latex] is already a candidate key of [latex]team[/latex] — and since every FD's left-hand side ([latex]name[/latex]) is already a superkey, [latex]team[/latex] is already in BCNF (and hence also in 3NF) even before decomposing. So both "team is NOT in BCNF" and "team is NOT in 3NF" are false.

Decomposing into [latex]t_1(name,city)[/latex] and [latex]t_2(name,owner)[/latex]: in each projection, [latex]name[/latex] remains a key (it determines the sole remaining attribute), so both [latex]t_1[/latex] and [latex]t_2[/latex] are trivially in BCNF. True.

For losslessness, the common attribute of the decomposition is [latex]name[/latex], and [latex]name\to city[/latex] (i.e. [latex]name[/latex] alone determines all of [latex]t_1[/latex]) — satisfying the standard lossless-join test ([latex]R_1\cap R_2[/latex] is a superkey of at least one of the two pieces). True.

Answer: t1 and t2 are in BCNF; and the decomposition is lossless.

Consider two relations describing teams and players in a sports league:

[latex]teams(tid, tname):tid, tname [/latex] are team-id and team-name, respectively
[latex]players(pid, pname, tid):pid,pname,tid[/latex] denote player-id, player-name and the team-id of the player, respectively

Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the name of the players who play for the team having name as 'MI'?
solution:
We want, for each player [latex]p[/latex] in [latex]\text{players}[/latex], their name, restricted to only those players whose [latex]tid[/latex] matches some team [latex]t[/latex] in [latex]\text{teams}[/latex] with [latex]t.tname=\text{'MI'}[/latex].

This is exactly:
[latex]\{p.pname\mid p\in players\ \wedge\ \exists t(t\in teams\ \wedge\ p.tid=t.tid\ \wedge\ t.tname=\text{'MI'})\}[/latex]

The key correctness checks: the outer variable [latex]p[/latex] must range over [latex]players[/latex] (not [latex]teams[/latex], since we want player names), and the join condition [latex]p.tid=t.tid[/latex] must actually be present inside the existential (options that drop this join condition would incorrectly return every player's name whenever team 'MI' exists at all, regardless of which team the player is actually on).

Answer: {p.pname | p∈players ∧ ∃t(t∈teams ∧ p.tid=t.tid ∧ t.tname='MI')}

A schedule of three database transactions [latex]T_1[/latex], [latex]T_2[/latex], and [latex]T_3[/latex] is shown. [latex]R_i(A)[/latex] and [latex]W_i(A)[/latex] denote read and write of data item [latex]A[/latex] by transaction [latex]T_i[/latex], [latex]i = 1, 2, 3[/latex]. The transaction [latex]T_1[/latex] aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?

[latex] R_1(X) \quad W_1(Y) \quad R_2(X) \quad R_2(Y) \quad R_3(Y) \quad ABORT(T_1)[/latex]
solution:
Schedule: [latex]R_1(X)\ W_1(Y)\ R_2(X)\ R_2(Y)\ R_3(Y)\ \text{ABORT}(T_1)[/latex].

[latex]T_1[/latex] writes [latex]Y[/latex] before aborting. Any transaction that subsequently read that (now-invalid) value of [latex]Y[/latex] has read "dirty" data and must be cascade-rolled-back:
- [latex]T_2[/latex] executes [latex]R_2(Y)[/latex] after [latex]W_1(Y)[/latex] — it read [latex]T_1[/latex]'s uncommitted write. [latex]T_2[/latex] must roll back.
- [latex]T_3[/latex] executes [latex]R_3(Y)[/latex] afterward too. Since no one else wrote [latex]Y[/latex] in between (only [latex]T_2[/latex] read it, without writing), [latex]T_3[/latex] also reads [latex]T_1[/latex]'s dirty value. [latex]T_3[/latex] must roll back as well.

Answer: Both T2 and T3

A functional dependency [latex]F:X \rightarrow Y[/latex] is termed as a useful functional dependency if and only if it satisfies all the following three conditions:

Consider a database of fixed-length records, stored as an ordered file. The database has 25,000 records, with each record being 100 bytes, of which the primary key occupies 15 bytes. The data file is block-aligned in that each data record is fully contained within a block. The database is indexed by a primary index file, which is also stored as a block-aligned ordered file. The figure below depicts this indexing scheme.

Suppose the block size of the file system is 1024 bytes, and a pointer to a block occupies 5 bytes. The system uses binary search on the index file to search for a record with a given key. You may assume that a binary search on an index file of [latex]b[/latex] blocks takes [latex]\left \lceil \log_2 b \right \rceil [/latex] block accesses in the worst case.
Given a key, the number of block accesses required to identify the block in the data file that may contain a record with the key, in the worst case, is _____
solution:
Compute the index size step by step:
- Records per data block = [latex]\lfloor1024/100\rfloor=10[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] data blocks = 25000 / 10 = 2500.
- Primary (sparse) index has one entry per data block: 2500 entries of [latex]15+5=20[/latex] bytes.
- Entries per index block = [latex]\lfloor1024/20\rfloor=51[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index blocks = [latex]\lceil2500/51\rceil=50[/latex].

Binary search on the index: [latex]\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6[/latex] block accesses identify the data block.

Answer: 6
